[Chapter 13 · Unsupervised Learning]{.eyebrow}

# Structure Without Labels

[Take a data set, seal the labels away, and see how much of the story the inputs alone can tell: PCA finds the directions, K-means finds the groups, and only then do we peek.]{.dek}
:::

Every other page on this site had a response to predict. Here there is none — or rather,
we lock it away. The plan: run [PCA]{.term} and [K-means]{.term} on a data set using
nothing but the inputs, and only at the end reveal the labels to measure how much
structure was sitting in $p(\mathbf{x})$ all along. The textbook's Chapter 13 reads both
methods as maximum likelihood with the labels treated as latent variables; this page runs
them, from scratch, in a few lines each.

::: {.defbox}
[Principal Directions]{.lbl}
[ S v = &lambda; v &nbsp;&mdash;&nbsp; the directions of a data cloud are the eigenvectors of its covariance ]{.math}
:::

## One direction at a time

Before the flowers, the book's own example (Section 13.1): four centered points, $(2, 1)$,
$(-2, -1)$, $(1, 2)$ and $(-1, -2)$, whose covariance is
$\mathbf{S} = \begin{bmatrix} 2.5 & 2 \\ 2 & 2.5 \end{bmatrix}$. Turn a direction $\mathbf{u}$
and watch two things: how much the points vary once projected onto it, $\mathbf{u}^\top\mathbf{S}\mathbf{u}$,
and what $\mathbf{S}$ does to $\mathbf{u}$ itself.

```{=html}
<script>
(function () {
  const root = document.getElementById('ix-pca'), L = window.LMIX, $ = s => root.querySelector(s);
  // The book's worked example (Section 13.1): four centered points.
  const P = [[2, 1], [-2, -1], [1, 2], [-1, -2]], m = P.length;
  const S = [[0, 0], [0, 0]];                                     // S = (1/m) sum x x^T
  P.forEach(p => { for (const i of [0, 1]) for (const j of [0, 1]) S[i][j] += p[i] * p[j] / m; });
  const tr = S[0][0] + S[1][1], det = S[0][0] * S[1][1] - S[0][1] ** 2, rad = Math.sqrt(tr * tr / 4 - det);
  const L1 = tr / 2 + rad, L2 = tr / 2 - rad;                     // eigenvalues
  const A1 = Math.atan2(L1 - S[0][0], S[0][1]) * 180 / Math.PI;   // angle of v1
  const A2 = A1 - 90;                                             // v2 is orthogonal
  const Su = u => [S[0][0] * u[0] + S[0][1] * u[1], S[1][0] * u[0] + S[1][1] * u[1]];
  let deg = 0;

  const R = 3.4, cx = 200, cy = 200, sc = 165 / R;               // data card: equal units
  const X = v => cx + v * sc, Y = v => cy - v * sc;
  function axes(svg, C, lim, scale, ticks) {
    const xs = v => cx + v * scale, ys = v => cy - v * scale;
    ticks.forEach(t => {
      L.el('line', { x1: xs(t), x2: xs(t), y1: ys(-lim), y2: ys(lim), stroke: C.grid }, svg);
      L.el('line', { x1: xs(-lim), x2: xs(lim), y1: ys(t), y2: ys(t), stroke: C.grid }, svg);
    });
    L.el('line', { x1: xs(-lim), x2: xs(lim), y1: ys(0), y2: ys(0), stroke: C.axis }, svg);
    L.el('line', { x1: xs(0), x2: xs(0), y1: ys(-lim), y2: ys(lim), stroke: C.axis }, svg);
    ticks.filter(t => t !== 0).forEach(t => {
      L.el('text', { x: xs(t), y: ys(0) + 17, 'text-anchor': 'middle', 'font-size': 14, fill: C.muted }, svg).textContent = t;
      L.el('text', { x: xs(0) - 6, y: ys(t) + 5, 'text-anchor': 'end', 'font-size': 14, fill: C.muted }, svg).textContent = t;
    });
  }
  function dataCard(C, u) {
    const svg = $('.ix-data'); svg.innerHTML = '';
    axes(svg, C, R, sc, [-3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3]);
    L.el('line', { x1: X(-R * u[0]), y1: Y(-R * u[1]), x2: X(R * u[0]), y2: Y(R * u[1]), stroke: C.fs, 'stroke-width': 2.2 }, svg);
    P.forEach(p => {
      const z = p[0] * u[0] + p[1] * u[1], q = [z * u[0], z * u[1]];      // score and its point on the line
      L.el('line', { x1: X(p[0]), y1: Y(p[1]), x2: X(q[0]), y2: Y(q[1]), stroke: C.red, 'stroke-width': 1.8, 'stroke-dasharray': '4 3' }, svg);
      L.el('circle', { cx: X(q[0]), cy: Y(q[1]), r: 5, fill: '#fff', stroke: C.fs, 'stroke-width': 2 }, svg);
    });
    P.forEach(p => L.el('circle', { cx: X(p[0]), cy: Y(p[1]), r: 7, fill: C.blue, stroke: '#fff', 'stroke-width': 2 }, svg));
    L.arrow(svg, [X(0), Y(0)], [X(u[0]), Y(u[1])], C.fs, 3);
    L.el('text', { x: X(1.18 * u[0]) + 4, y: Y(1.18 * u[1]) + 5, 'font-size': 17, 'font-style': 'italic', fill: C.fs }, svg).textContent = 'u';
  }
  const RM = 5, sm = 165 / RM;                                    // matrix card: room for Su up to 4.5
  const XM = v => cx + v * sm, YM = v => cy - v * sm;
  function matCard(C, u, w) {
    const svg = $('.ix-mat'); svg.innerHTML = '';
    axes(svg, C, RM, sm, [-4, -2, 0, 2, 4]);
    const circ = [], ell = [];
    for (let k = 0; k <= 120; k++) {
      const t = 2 * Math.PI * k / 120, c = [Math.cos(t), Math.sin(t)], e = Su(c);
      circ.push(XM(c[0]) + ',' + YM(c[1])); ell.push(XM(e[0]) + ',' + YM(e[1]));
    }
    L.el('polygon', { points: ell.join(' '), fill: C.plane, stroke: C.cyan, 'stroke-width': 1.6 }, svg);
    L.el('polyline', { points: circ.join(' '), fill: 'none', stroke: C.muted, 'stroke-width': 1.2, 'stroke-dasharray': '4 4' }, svg);
    L.arrow(svg, [XM(0), YM(0)], [XM(w[0]), YM(w[1])], C.orange, 3);
    L.arrow(svg, [XM(0), YM(0)], [XM(u[0]), YM(u[1])], C.fs, 3);
    L.el('text', { x: XM(w[0]) + (w[0] >= 0 ? 6 : -6), y: YM(w[1]) - 6, 'text-anchor': w[0] >= 0 ? 'start' : 'end', 'font-size': 17, 'font-style': 'italic', fill: C.orange }, svg).textContent = 'Su';
    L.el('text', { x: XM(1.35 * u[0]) + (u[0] >= 0 ? 4 : -4), y: YM(1.35 * u[1]) + 5, 'text-anchor': u[0] >= 0 ? 'start' : 'end', 'font-size': 17, 'font-style': 'italic', fill: C.fs }, svg).textContent = 'u';
  }
  function matrixLine(C, u, w) {                                  // S u = Su, as numbers
    const td = (x, color) => '<td' + (color ? ' style="color:' + color + '"' : '') + '>' + x + '</td>';
    const col = (v, color) => '<table><tr>' + td(L.fmt(v[0]), color) + '</tr><tr>' + td(L.fmt(v[1]), color) + '</tr></table>';
    const mat = '<table><tr>' + td(L.fmt(S[0][0], 1)) + td(L.fmt(S[0][1], 1)) + '</tr><tr>' + td(L.fmt(S[1][0], 1)) + td(L.fmt(S[1][1], 1)) + '</tr></table>';
    $('.m-su').innerHTML = mat + col(u, C.fs) + '<span class="lhs">=</span>' + col(w, C.orange);
  }
  const near = (a, b) => Math.abs(((a - b + 90) % 180 + 180) % 180 - 90) < 0.75;
  function note(v, turn) {
    if (near(deg, A1)) return 'This is v₁ = (1, 1)/√2. S does not turn it, only stretches it: Su = 4.5u. That 4.5 is the most variance any direction captures, 90% of the total. All four points land on just two scores, ±3/√2 ≈ ±2.12, because they come in mirror-image pairs about this line; what the projection discards is their spread along v₂.';
    if (near(deg, A2)) return 'This is v₂ = (1, −1)/√2, the other direction S does not turn: Su = 0.5u. It captures the least variance of any direction, the 10% that v₁ leaves.';
    return 'S turns u by ' + L.fmt(turn, 1) + '°, toward the long axis of the ellipse. Rotate u until S stops turning it: the directions it only stretches are its eigenvectors, and the variance along u peaks at one of them.';
  }
  function update() {
    const C = L.colors(root), a = deg * Math.PI / 180, u = [Math.cos(a), Math.sin(a)], w = Su(u);
    const v = u[0] * w[0] + u[1] * w[1];                          // u^T S u, the variance along u
    const turn = Math.abs(Math.atan2(u[0] * w[1] - u[1] * w[0], u[0] * w[0] + u[1] * w[1])) * 180 / Math.PI;
    dataCard(C, u); matCard(C, u, w); matrixLine(C, u, w);
    L.stat($('.t-var'), v, near(deg, A1), x => L.fmt(x, 2));
    L.stat($('.t-share'), v / tr, near(deg, A1), x => Math.round(100 * x) + '%');
    L.stat($('.t-turn'), turn, turn < 0.75, x => L.fmt(x, 1) + '°');
    $('.ix-note').textContent = note(v, turn);
  }
  const sl = L.slider($('.ix-a'), $('.ix-av'), v => L.fmt(v, 1) + '°', v => { deg = v; update(); });
  L.presets($('.ix-buttons'), [
    { label: 'Horizontal (0°)', action: () => sl.set(0) },
    { label: 'v₁ (45°)', action: () => sl.set(A1) },
    { label: 'v₂ (−45°)', action: () => sl.set(A2) },
  ]);
  sl.refresh();
})();
</script>
</div>
```

## The data, with the labels sealed

We use Fisher's irises: 150 flowers, four measurements each, three species. It is the
classic *labeled* data set — which makes it perfect for this experiment, because we can
withhold the species column now and audit ourselves against it later. The four features
are standardized first; PCA is not scale-invariant, and we want each measurement to speak
with equal weight.

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}

## Python

## Principal components, by hand

Three lines: form the sample covariance, take its eigenvectors, project. The first two
components carry 95.8% of the variance — four correlated measurements were, all along,
close to a two-dimensional story. The right panel is the scree plot the figure at the top
promised: each component's share, and the running total.

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}

## Python
```{pyodide}
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Same sealed data as the first cell: every cell here stands on its own.
# Fisher's irises, 150 flowers: four measurements in millimeters (two digits
# each) and the species (one digit, 0-2), nine digits per flower.
IRIS = ("513514020493014020473213020463115020503614020543917040463414030503415020"
        "442914020493115010543715020483416020483014010433011010584012020574415040"
        "543913040513514030573817030513815030543417020513715040463610020513317050"
        "483419020503016020503416040523515020523414020473216020483116020543415040"
        "524115010554214020493115020503212020553513020493614010443013020513415020"
        "503513030452313030443213020503516060513819040483014030513816020463214020"
        "533715020503314020703247141643245151693149151552340131652846151572845131"
        "633347161492433101662946131522739141502035101593042151602240101612947141"
        "562936131673144141563045151582741101622245151562539111593248181612840131"
        "632549151612847121642943131663044141682848141673050171602945151572635101"
        "552438111552437101582739121602751161543045151603445161673147151632344131"
        "563041131552540131552644121613046141582640121502333101562742131573042121"
        "572942131622943131512530111572841131633360252582751192713059212632956182"
        "653058222763066212492545172732963182672558182723661252653251202642753192"
        "683055212572550202582851242643253232653055182773867222772669232602250152"
        "693257232562849202772867202632749182673357212723260182622848182613049182"
        "642856212723058162742861192793864202642856222632851152612656142773061232"
        "633456242643155182603048182693154212673156242693151232582751192683259232"
        "673357252673052232632550192653052202623454232593051182")
rows = np.array([[int(IRIS[i + j:i + j + 2]) for j in (0, 2, 4, 6)] + [int(IRIS[i + 8])]
                 for i in range(0, len(IRIS), 9)])
X_raw, species_sealed = rows[:, :4] / 10, rows[:, 4]
X = (X_raw - X_raw.mean(axis=0)) / X_raw.std(axis=0)

S = X.T @ X / len(X)                   # 4 x 4 sample covariance
evals, evecs = np.linalg.eigh(S)
evals, evecs = evals[::-1], evecs[:, ::-1]      # largest first
evecs = evecs * np.sign(evecs[0, :])   # fix signs (cosmetic)

frac = evals / evals.sum()
for k in range(4):
    print(f"PC{k+1}: {frac[k]:5.1%}   cumulative {frac[:k+1].sum():5.1%}")

Z = X @ evecs[:, :2]                   # every flower gets two coordinates

fig, (axZ, axS) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4.4))
axZ.scatter(Z[:, 0], Z[:, 1], s=45, color="#076FA1", alpha=0.7,
            edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.6)
axZ.set_xlabel("first principal score"); axZ.set_ylabel("second principal score")
axZ.set_title("150 flowers, no labels")

# Scree plot: each component's share of the variance, and the running total
axS.bar(np.arange(1, 5), frac, width=0.6, color="#076FA1", label="share of variance")
axS.plot(np.arange(1, 5), np.cumsum(frac), "o-", color="#31417A", lw=1.6, label="cumulative")
axS.set_xticks([1, 2, 3, 4]); axS.set_xticklabels(["PC1", "PC2", "PC3", "PC4"])
axS.set_ylim(0, 1.05); axS.set_ylabel("share of total variance")
axS.set_title("Scree plot"); axS.legend(loc="center right", fontsize=8)
for ax in (axZ, axS):
    for s in ["top", "right"]: ax.spines[s].set_visible(False)
    ax.grid(axis="y", color="#e6e3da", lw=0.8); ax.set_axisbelow(True)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

## R
```{webr}
# Same sealed data as the first cell: every cell here stands on its own.
X_raw <- as.matrix(iris[, 1:4])
species_sealed <- iris$Species
X <- scale(X_raw)

S <- t(X) %*% X / nrow(X)              # 4 x 4 sample covariance
e <- eigen(S)                          # largest first by default
frac <- e$values / sum(e$values)
for (k in 1:4) cat(sprintf("PC%d: %5.1f%%   cumulative %5.1f%%\n",
                           k, 100 * frac[k], 100 * sum(frac[1:k])))

V <- e$vectors
V <- sweep(V, 2, sign(V[1, ]), "*")    # fix signs (cosmetic)
Z <- X %*% V[, 1:2]                    # every flower gets two coordinates

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(Z, pch = 19, col = adjustcolor("#076FA1", 0.7), cex = 1.1, bty = "l",
     xlab = "first principal score", ylab = "second principal score",
     main = "150 flowers, no labels")
grid(col = "#e6e3da", lty = 1, lwd = 0.6)

# Scree plot: each component's share of the variance, and the running total
mids <- barplot(frac, names.arg = paste0("PC", 1:4), col = "#076FA1", border = NA,
                ylim = c(0, 1.05), ylab = "share of total variance", main = "Scree plot")
grid(col = "#e6e3da", lty = 1, lwd = 0.6)
lines(mids, cumsum(frac), type = "o", pch = 19, col = "#31417A", lwd = 1.6)
legend("right", c("share of variance", "cumulative"), col = c("#076FA1", "#31417A"),
       pch = c(15, 19), lty = c(NA, 1), lwd = c(NA, 1.6), pt.cex = c(1.6, 1), bty = "n", cex = 0.8)
```

:::

Even with one color, the plot is not one blob: a tight island sits apart from a long
ridge. We did not put that there. It is structure in $p(\mathbf{x})$, and the next step
gives it names — well, numbers.

## The book's worked example

Before the flowers, the chapter's own example: six points on a line, $\{0, 1, 2, 7, 8, 9\}$,
$K = 2$, and the deliberately poor start $\mu_1 = 0$, $\mu_2 = 1$. The trace should match the
book's $150 \to 53.2 \to 27.28 \to 4$, ending at centers 1 and 8.

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}

## Python
```{pyodide}
import numpy as np

x = np.array([0., 1., 2., 7., 8., 9.])
mu = np.array([0., 1.])                     # the book's deliberately poor start
J = lambda c: ((x - mu[c]) ** 2).sum()

c = np.abs(x[:, None] - mu).argmin(axis=1)  # first assignment
trace = [J(c)]
while True:
    mu = np.array([x[c == k].mean() for k in range(2)])   # update
    trace.append(J(c))
    c_new = np.abs(x[:, None] - mu).argmin(axis=1)        # reassign
    if (c_new == c).all():
        break                               # no assignment changed: halt
    c = c_new
    trace.append(J(c))
print("J:", " -> ".join(f"{j:g}" for j in trace))   # the book: 150 -> 53.2 -> 27.28 -> 4
print("centers:", mu)
```

## R
```{webr}
x <- c(0, 1, 2, 7, 8, 9)
mu <- c(0, 1)                               # the book's deliberately poor start
J <- function(cl) sum((x - mu[cl])^2)
nearest <- function() max.col(-abs(outer(x, mu, "-")), ties.method = "first")

cl <- nearest()                             # first assignment
trace <- J(cl)
repeat {
  mu <- sapply(1:2, function(k) mean(x[cl == k]))   # update
  trace <- c(trace, J(cl))
  cl_new <- nearest()                               # reassign
  if (all(cl_new == cl)) break              # no assignment changed: halt
  cl <- cl_new
  trace <- c(trace, J(cl))
}
cat("J:", paste(format(trace, drop0trailing = TRUE, trim = TRUE), collapse = " -> "), "\n")
cat("centers:", mu, "\n")
```

:::

## K-means, by hand

Lloyd's algorithm is two alternating steps: assign each point to its nearest center, move
each center to the mean of its points. Neither step can raise the objective $J$, so the
printed trace never rises and then stops moving — the same monotone descent as
the worked example above, on real data.

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}

## Python
```{pyodide}
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Same sealed data as the first cell: every cell here stands on its own.
# Fisher's irises, 150 flowers: four measurements in millimeters (two digits
# each) and the species (one digit, 0-2), nine digits per flower.
IRIS = ("513514020493014020473213020463115020503614020543917040463414030503415020"
        "442914020493115010543715020483416020483014010433011010584012020574415040"
        "543913040513514030573817030513815030543417020513715040463610020513317050"
        "483419020503016020503416040523515020523414020473216020483116020543415040"
        "524115010554214020493115020503212020553513020493614010443013020513415020"
        "503513030452313030443213020503516060513819040483014030513816020463214020"
        "533715020503314020703247141643245151693149151552340131652846151572845131"
        "633347161492433101662946131522739141502035101593042151602240101612947141"
        "562936131673144141563045151582741101622245151562539111593248181612840131"
        "632549151612847121642943131663044141682848141673050171602945151572635101"
        "552438111552437101582739121602751161543045151603445161673147151632344131"
        "563041131552540131552644121613046141582640121502333101562742131573042121"
        "572942131622943131512530111572841131633360252582751192713059212632956182"
        "653058222763066212492545172732963182672558182723661252653251202642753192"
        "683055212572550202582851242643253232653055182773867222772669232602250152"
        "693257232562849202772867202632749182673357212723260182622848182613049182"
        "642856212723058162742861192793864202642856222632851152612656142773061232"
        "633456242643155182603048182693154212673156242693151232582751192683259232"
        "673357252673052232632550192653052202623454232593051182")
rows = np.array([[int(IRIS[i + j:i + j + 2]) for j in (0, 2, 4, 6)] + [int(IRIS[i + 8])]
                 for i in range(0, len(IRIS), 9)])
X_raw, species_sealed = rows[:, :4] / 10, rows[:, 4]
X = (X_raw - X_raw.mean(axis=0)) / X_raw.std(axis=0)
evals, evecs = np.linalg.eigh(X.T @ X / len(X))    # the projection from above
Z = X @ evecs[:, ::-1]

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
K = 3
mus = Z[rng.choice(len(Z), K, replace=False)]   # init: three random flowers

for it in range(6):
    d2 = ((Z[:, None, :] - mus[None, :, :]) ** 2).sum(axis=2)
    cluster = d2.argmin(axis=1)                  # assign
    J = d2[np.arange(len(Z)), cluster].sum()
    print(f"iteration {it + 1}:  J = {J:6.1f}")
    for k in range(K):                           # update
        mus[k] = Z[cluster == k].mean(axis=0)
```

## R
```{webr}
# Same sealed data as the first cell: every cell here stands on its own.
X_raw <- as.matrix(iris[, 1:4])
species_sealed <- iris$Species
X <- scale(X_raw)
e <- eigen(t(X) %*% X / nrow(X), symmetric = TRUE)  # the projection from above
Z <- X %*% e$vectors

set.seed(1)
K <- 3
mus <- Z[sample(nrow(Z), K), ]                   # init: three random flowers

for (it in 1:6) {
  d2 <- outer(rowSums(Z^2), rep(1, K)) - 2 * Z %*% t(mus) +
        outer(rep(1, nrow(Z)), rowSums(mus^2))
  cluster <- max.col(-d2)                        # assign
  J <- sum(d2[cbind(seq_len(nrow(Z)), cluster)])
  cat(sprintf("iteration %d:  J = %6.1f\n", it, J))
  for (k in 1:K)                                 # update
    mus[k, ] <- colMeans(Z[cluster == k, , drop = FALSE])
}
```

:::

The two languages start from different random centers, so the traces differ, but both
settle near $J \approx 139$–$141$ within a few iterations. Convergence is guaranteed;
convergence to the *best* partition is not, which is why production implementations
(`sklearn.cluster.KMeans`, R's `kmeans` with `nstart`) run several restarts and keep the
best. The textbook's statistical reading explains what we just fit: a Gaussian mixture
with equal weights and a shared spherical covariance whose variance has been sent to zero — density estimation with the class
labels treated as missing data.

## Breaking the seal

Now, and only now, we look at the species.

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}

## Python
```{pyodide}
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Same sealed data as the first cell: every cell here stands on its own.
# Fisher's irises, 150 flowers: four measurements in millimeters (two digits
# each) and the species (one digit, 0-2), nine digits per flower.
IRIS = ("513514020493014020473213020463115020503614020543917040463414030503415020"
        "442914020493115010543715020483416020483014010433011010584012020574415040"
        "543913040513514030573817030513815030543417020513715040463610020513317050"
        "483419020503016020503416040523515020523414020473216020483116020543415040"
        "524115010554214020493115020503212020553513020493614010443013020513415020"
        "503513030452313030443213020503516060513819040483014030513816020463214020"
        "533715020503314020703247141643245151693149151552340131652846151572845131"
        "633347161492433101662946131522739141502035101593042151602240101612947141"
        "562936131673144141563045151582741101622245151562539111593248181612840131"
        "632549151612847121642943131663044141682848141673050171602945151572635101"
        "552438111552437101582739121602751161543045151603445161673147151632344131"
        "563041131552540131552644121613046141582640121502333101562742131573042121"
        "572942131622943131512530111572841131633360252582751192713059212632956182"
        "653058222763066212492545172732963182672558182723661252653251202642753192"
        "683055212572550202582851242643253232653055182773867222772669232602250152"
        "693257232562849202772867202632749182673357212723260182622848182613049182"
        "642856212723058162742861192793864202642856222632851152612656142773061232"
        "633456242643155182603048182693154212673156242693151232582751192683259232"
        "673357252673052232632550192653052202623454232593051182")
rows = np.array([[int(IRIS[i + j:i + j + 2]) for j in (0, 2, 4, 6)] + [int(IRIS[i + 8])]
                 for i in range(0, len(IRIS), 9)])
X_raw, species_sealed = rows[:, :4] / 10, rows[:, 4]
X = (X_raw - X_raw.mean(axis=0)) / X_raw.std(axis=0)
evals, evecs = np.linalg.eigh(X.T @ X / len(X))    # the projection from above
evecs = evecs[:, ::-1]
evecs = evecs * np.sign(evecs[0, :])               # same signs as the first plot
Z = X @ evecs

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)                     # the clustering from above
K = 3
mus = Z[rng.choice(len(Z), K, replace=False)]
for _ in range(6):
    d2 = ((Z[:, None, :] - mus[None, :, :]) ** 2).sum(axis=2)
    cluster = d2.argmin(axis=1)
    for k in range(K):
        mus[k] = Z[cluster == k].mean(axis=0)

names = ["setosa", "versicolor", "virginica"]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 5))
for s, color in zip(range(3), ["#076FA1", "#3EB489", "#9E4F00"]):
    pts = Z[species_sealed == s]
    ax.scatter(pts[:, 0], pts[:, 1], s=45, color=color, alpha=0.75,
               edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.6, label=names[s])
ax.set_xlabel("first principal score"); ax.set_ylabel("second principal score")
ax.set_title("The same cloud, species revealed")
ax.legend()
for s in ["top", "right"]: ax.spines[s].set_visible(False)
ax.grid(axis="y", color="#e6e3da", lw=0.8); ax.set_axisbelow(True)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

# How well did the clusters anticipate the species?
tab = np.zeros((3, 3), dtype=int)
for k, s in zip(cluster, species_sealed):
    tab[k, s] += 1
print("cluster x species:\n", tab)
print(f"purity: {tab.max(axis=1).sum() / len(Z):.1%}")
```

## R
```{webr}
# Same sealed data as the first cell: every cell here stands on its own.
X_raw <- as.matrix(iris[, 1:4])
species_sealed <- iris$Species
X <- scale(X_raw)
e <- eigen(t(X) %*% X / nrow(X), symmetric = TRUE)  # the projection from above
V <- sweep(e$vectors, 2, sign(e$vectors[1, ]), "*") # same signs as the first plot
Z <- X %*% V

set.seed(1)                                        # the clustering from above
K <- 3
mus <- Z[sample(nrow(Z), K), ]
for (it in 1:6) {
  d2 <- sapply(1:K, function(k) rowSums(sweep(Z, 2, mus[k, ])^2))
  cluster <- max.col(-d2)
  for (k in 1:K) mus[k, ] <- colMeans(Z[cluster == k, , drop = FALSE])
}

cols <- c("#076FA1", "#3EB489", "#9E4F00")
plot(Z, pch = 19, cex = 1.1, bty = "l",
     col = adjustcolor(cols[as.integer(species_sealed)], 0.75),
     xlab = "first principal score", ylab = "second principal score",
     main = "The same cloud, species revealed")
grid(col = "#e6e3da", lty = 1, lwd = 0.6)
legend("topright", levels(species_sealed), col = cols, pch = 19, bty = "n")

# How well did the clusters anticipate the species?
tab <- table(cluster = cluster, species = species_sealed)
print(tab)
cat(sprintf("purity: %.1f%%\n", 100 * sum(apply(tab, 1, max)) / nrow(Z)))
```

:::

The audit is instructive in both directions. One cluster captures *setosa* almost
perfectly — that was the island. The other two clusters split *versicolor* and
*virginica* imperfectly, because along the ridge the two species genuinely overlap in
these four measurements. Purity comes out around 85%: most of the class structure was in
$p(\mathbf{x})$ before any label was used, and the part that wasn't is exactly the part
where the species are hard to tell apart, labels in hand or not.

## The full-scale version

The textbook's applied exercise runs this same experiment at scale: 10,000 Fashion-MNIST
images with the labels sealed, PCA on the sample covariance, $K$-means cluster averages you
can recognize as trousers and boots, and a small PyTorch [autoencoder]{.term} whose learned
two-dimensional code bends where PCA's cannot. Just over half the images end up in a cluster
whose dominant class is their own — from an analysis that never saw a label — but the
garments that separate and the ones that do not are worth studying separately.

[**Applied — Unsupervised Fashion-MNIST**](ch13_02_applied.qmd) walks through it, and opens
in Google Colab.

::: {.explore}
[Try it]{.lbl}
Set `K = 2` and rerun the clustering. Lloyd's algorithm will happily produce two clusters —
it always converges, whatever $K$ you assert. Then try `K = 4`. The textbook's
mixture-model reading turns "which $K$ is right?" into ordinary model selection with
held-out likelihood; with $K$-means alone you are left staring at the objective. Feel that
difference here.
:::
